tweets.text: RT @KhurramDara: The Reg Crypto release spills A LOT of ink on the history/background here and the sequence of events leading up to this proposal. Many folks will understandably gloss over it but it's pretty important because it can help reduce litigation/political/narrative risk. We'll probably see some headlines or spin from critics that characterizes Reg Crypto as an industry "giveaway" or somehow ties it to CLARITY and implies this was done on a whim. Very, very far from it... The release explains the SEC's approach to crypto pre-2025 and the "regulation by enforcement" era, and then lays out how beginning in 2025 the SEC: -Established the crypto task force -Held a series of roundtables and took meetings with the public -Solicited written public input on specific questions (re security status, what should be scoped out, public offerings, safe harbor from registration, among others) -Began issuing staff statements to provide clarity on a range of topics (e.g. memecoins, mining, staking, liquid staking, tokenized securities) -Participated in the PWG which specifically recommended the SEC develop fit for purpose rules and a safe harbor -Launched Project Crypto -Then in 2026 released interpretive guidance on the application of securities laws to crypto assets All of this led up to yesterday's release of Regulation Crypto Assets. And even in this release, there are 140+ questions the SEC is seeking comment from the public on. The SEC is making it clear that this is a thoughtful and deliberative proposal that was a product of a transparent and public process, not just something they threw up because commission leadership or this admin wants them to be "pro crypto." Will be extremely helpful in case Reg Crypto becomes a political football or other industry groups attempt to challenge it.

tweets.text: This is a cool account of what changes when tokenization moves beyond wrappers. Once assets share a programmable settlement layer, markets can organize around the economic relationships among those assets, instead of routing everything through dollars because legacy infrastructure requires it. Correlated pairs explain where liquidity should sit, but the next (and more interesting IMO) question is how capital gets there. A vault can take assets investors already want to own and allocate them across correlated AMM pairs, lending markets and bridge liquidity, subject to transparent risk limits. Idle capital can earn lending yield when it is not needed for swaps, and long-term holders can supply liquidity without recreating the balance sheet and infrastructure of a traditional market-making firm. Think about it - market making can become just a native portfolio function. Meaning the same capital can serve as an investment position, trading liquidity, and collateral. Tokenization and infra like vaults will change how capital itself is organized and used.

tweets.text: RT @L0laL33tz: You’ve heard of Chainalysis suing the US over an ICE surveillance contract. What you haven’t heard is what the task force that set out the contract is actually about. The US used to dismantle drug networks by prosecuting them. For 40 years that was OCDETF, a Justice Department program that put federal prosecutors at the center of every major transnational crime investigation. It was shut down last year. 30 permanent Homeland Security Task Forces replaced it, created by executive order, with the governing role delegated to Homeland Security Investigations, the law enforcement arm of ICE, and the second largest investigative agency in the US. The new model, in the words of OCDETF's former director Thomas Padden, "eliminates the role of prosecutors.” Its termination, Padden wrote, "comes as the Trump Administration ceases the United States' lawful maritime drug interdiction mission in favor of its questionable use of military strikes against alleged drug smuggling vessels." Padden warned Congress in March that with prosecutors out of the loop, information sharing between law enforcement, the intelligence community and the military is "unclear." Now the task forces that inherited the OCDETF’s casework are buying blockchain surveillance tools at a record level. The ICE contract Chainalysis is suing over is the largest such contract in US history and roughly three-quarters of everything the US government has ever spent on blockchain tracing with a single contractor. According to ICE’s statement of need, the tools are meant to help the task forces Cybercrime Disruption Center (CDC) to combat cybercrime. But the CDC doesn’t even seem to have a website, nor are cybercrime disruptions listed as a core responsibility of the HSTF. In effect, it seems that the CDC does not exist at all in public view apart from its procurement records. For context, ICE’s HSI is the same agency Senator Ron Wyden asked the DOJ to investigate in 2023 after it obtained millions of Americans' money transfer records, which he described as “mass surveillance.” The same agency documented monitoring lawful protests, pulling demonstrators into unmarked vans, accused of unproportionately targeting people of color, and painting immigrant youth as gang members with questionable evidence. Whoever wins the contract battle, an HSI cybercrime center without a website now has close to $100M in blockchain surveillance capabilities.

tweets.text: RT @JBSDC: Cheat sheet for everyone: - Rule text starts on page 320 and ends on 355, everything before that is commentary, after is paperwork/appendices. - Crypto asset (324) is defined as any digital representation of value recorded on a cryptographically-secured distribution layer, but this only applies to subject crypto assets, which are those subject to a "covered investment contract." @NYcryptolawyer's ineluctable modalities point is now in regulation - SEC is saying that a firm attempting to comply with this regulation in good faith shouldn't face enforcement actions (325). - Up to $75 million of a covered crypto security can be sold each year (333).
